a2fbfc58918940d6.text: Labels are texts too. A food packet is a text with two audiences. The front is for the shopper walking past: bright colours, a big name and claims like “high in fibre”. Its job is to sell. The back and sides are there to inform, and the law says certain facts must be there. Health Star Rating. From half a star up to five. More stars means a healthier choice, but only compare similar foods, like cereal with cereal. Ingredients. Listed from the most to the least. If sugar is near the start, there's a lot of it. Nutrition panel. A table of what's inside, per serve and per 100 g. Use per 100 g to compare two products fairly, because serve sizes are different. Allergens. Foods like peanuts, milk, egg and wheat must be shown. Many packs have a “Contains:” line. Dates. A use-by date is about safety: don't eat it after that day. A best-before date is about quality: it may still be fine after. You don't read a label from top to bottom. You scan it: decide what you need, go straight to that part, and check.

472c592af60c8e8e.text: The Health Star Rating. Food labels can be hard to read in a hurry. So the Australian, state and territory and New Zealand governments built a shortcut: the Health Star Rating. It started in June 2014. The rating goes from half a star to five stars. It's worked out from what's in 100 g or 100 mL of the food: things like energy, saturated fat, sugar and sodium, and also fibre, protein, and fruit, vegetables, nuts and legumes. The official advice is to compare similar foods, found in the same part of the supermarket. Compare a cereal with a cereal, not a cereal with a yoghurt. It has limits. The system is voluntary, so not every product shows it. And it doesn't count everything, like vitamins or how the food was made. Think about it. Who made the Health Star Rating, and why? Why should you only compare similar foods? What does “voluntary” mean, and why does it matter?

6f09e2ea8f1d073f.text: Labels are texts too. A food packet is a text written for two audiences with two purposes. The front targets a shopper who will glance at it for a second or two: colour, branding and claims such as “high in fibre” are designed to persuade. The back and sides inform, and food standards law requires certain information to be there. Health Star Rating. A rating from half a star to five that summarises the overall nutrition of a packaged food. It's only useful when comparing similar products. Ingredients. Listed in order of weight, from most to least, so the first few tell you what you're mostly eating. Nutrition information panel. Average amounts per serve and per 100 g. Serve sizes vary between brands, so per 100 g is the fair comparison. Allergens. Common allergens such as peanuts, milk, egg and wheat must be declared, often in a “Contains:” statement. Dates. A use-by date is a safety limit; a best-before date is a quality guide. Skilled readers don't read labels in order. They scan with a purpose: decide what they need, locate the right section, and check the detail.

e926cdcf7effc31e.text: The Health Star Rating. Nutrition panels are dense, and shoppers make decisions in seconds. To bridge that gap, the Australian, state and territory and New Zealand governments introduced the Health Star Rating system in June 2014. The rating runs from half a star to five stars and is calculated per 100 g or 100 mL. It weighs energy, saturated fat, sugar and sodium against positive components such as fibre, protein, and fruit, vegetables, nuts and legumes. The official guidance is to use it only to compare similar products from the same part of the supermarket. The system has limits. It is voluntary, so many products don't display it, and it doesn't account for everything, such as vitamins and minerals or how a food is processed. It's a shortcut, not the whole story. Think about it. Who made the Health Star Rating, and why? Why should you only compare similar foods? What does “voluntary” mean, and why does it matter?
